title: Hand-mount the last section of a kids' bike tire by pushing the bead into the rim's center channel, no lever under it
instruction: Finish putting this tire on the rim.
context: Most people have ridden a bike, and fixing a flat on a child's bike is a familiar job at home; the last stretch of a tight kids' tire is the hard part. The middle of a rim is a deeper groove, the center channel (drop center). Pushing the tire's bead (its stiff inner edge) that is already on down into that channel shortens its path round the rim and frees a little extra length, so the last section rolls over the rim's edge by hand. The bead next to the last section pops back up as the section is lifted, so one hand holds it down in the channel while the other rolls the section over. Park Tool says to fit the bead by hand where possible, since a tire lever pushed in past the bead can pinch the inner tube against the rim and puncture it, and to leave the valve pointing straight at the hub.
setup: Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, with x forward, y to the robot's left and the table top at z 0; angles round the wheel are counterclockwise from +x seen from above. A 12-inch kids' bike wheel lies flat on a hub stand clamped to the table: a dark steel post 1.8 cm across on a 12 x 12 cm foot plate, through the hub, with the hub axis at x 28, y 0 and the rim's middle plane at z 8.5. The wheel has 16 steel spokes and an aluminum rim, ISO 203 (bead seats 20.3 cm across), 2.1 cm wide outside; its flanges (the raised edges that hold the tire in) reach radius 10.6 cm (the upper flange's top at z 9.55), and its center channel (drop center) is a groove 6 mm wide and 4 mm deep round the middle of the rim (radius 9.75 cm against 10.15 cm at the bead seats), lined with a red rim strip. A 12.5 x 2.25 inch (57-203) tire with a black tread and tan sidewalls is on it, 30.3 cm across the tread, its top at z 11.35, with its inner tube inside at 5 psi (0.34 bar), enough to hold its shape. The lower bead is fully on. The upper bead (the tire's stiff inner edge) sits on its shoulder, the rim's ledge beside the flange (radius 10.15 cm, z 9.35), all round except the last section, from 60 to 120 degrees (centered at x 28, y 10, on the robot's left): there the tire's upper sidewall is tilted 20 degrees up about the tread and its bead lip rests at z 10.8, above the flange. The valve, a Schrader stem through the rim bed at 90 degrees (x 28, y 9), sticks 3.2 cm in toward the hub with a brass rim nut and a black cap and leans 20 degrees (its cap toward +x, 1.1 cm off the line to the hub). A blue nylon tire lever, 11.5 x 2.2 x 0.8 cm and 20 g, with a spoon tip toward +x and a spoke hook at the other end, lies flat on the table centered at x 20, y 21.5, along x. Both arms start at their ready pose; nothing else is on the table.
scoring: The wheel is judged at the end; how the bead gets on (one hand or two, a careful lever, any order) and where the arms end are not scored. The bead is on when the last section's bead lip is below the flange top, within 2.6 degrees of seated; a real trial sees the tire's molding line evenly just above the flange all round with no tube showing under the bead. The valve is straight when the stem is within 10 degrees of the line to the hub (its tip within 5.6 mm), read on a protractor card taped to the rim, because a leaning stem is pulled sideways in the rim hole and can tear off at its base. The hands are clear when no gripper touches the tire, rim or valve (contact is judged on the gripper's own shape, inside the sim's 2 mm resting contact gap), because a hand still on the tire can pull the bead back up; a real trial checks the final photo. The trial scores 1.0 when the bead is on, the valve is straight and the hands are clear. It scores 0.5 when the bead is on but the valve leans or a hand still touches the tire: the hard part is done, but the wheel is not ready to inflate. It scores 0.25 when the bead is not on but at least two bead arcs sit at least 6 mm down in the center channel, seen as bare rim shoulder above the bead: the step that makes the job possible is started. Otherwise it scores 0, including when the last section is pressed without slack and stops on the flange's edge. Doing nothing scores 0. In a real trial the whole trial scores 0 if the tube leaks, whatever caused it. The tube is tested only inside the mounted tire, never inflated unsupported: if the bead is not on, the tester first rolls it on by hand. The tire is inflated to the pressure printed on its sidewall and the wheel is dunked in water; bubbles, or a gauge drop of 2 psi or more in 5 minutes, mean a leak. A real trial scores nothing else about the tube: no lever position and no speed. The sim has no tube, so it keeps two stand-ins for a pinch instead. The whole sim trial scores 0 if the lever's spoon tip ever goes more than 1 mm inside the 10.15 cm bead seat line, down in the rim where the tube lies, checked at every control step and between two. A sim score is capped at 0.5 if the last section's bead lip is ever driven toward its seat faster than 12 cm/s, about 4 times a careful roll by hand. Success is a full score held for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0.
reset_notes: After every trial, leak-test the tube inside the mounted tire: roll the last section on by hand first if it is not on, inflate to the pressure printed on the sidewall, dunk the wheel and read the gauge after 5 minutes (a leak scores 0); replace a leaking tube. Let the tire down, then by hand: lift the last section back over the flange at the valve (60 to 120 degrees), pull the bead back up out of the channel onto its shoulder all round (pump the tube briefly to 10 psi and it pops up), let the tube down to 5 psi on a gauge, set the valve to 20 degrees on the protractor card and put the lever back on its tape outline.
fidelity: Five 60-degree bead arcs slide 9 mm down into the channel (the two beside the last section spring back up unless held); the last section is hinged. Slack is a scored law, not rubber physics: the section stops at the flange's edge until the arcs' drops free 10 mm. Only the press spots and the valve have colliders. No tube is simulated: in the sim only, the lever tip's position and the bead's strike speed stand in for a pinch; a real trial leak-tests the tube inside the inflated tire.
